species.name: Greater mousedeer
species.fact: The decisive 2008 rediscovery photographs showed the throat and chest markings needed to identify the species.
species.summary: A small hoofed forest browser with a rounded body and very slender legs. Its rediscovery on Pulau Ubin shows why an animal missing from casual sightings is not necessarily gone.
species.identification: Reddish-brown fur, pale underparts and contrasting throat markings. More robust than the lesser mousedeer; useful photographs show the neck and chest, not just apparent size. It has no antlers.
species.diet: Fallen fruit, tender leaves and other low-growing plant material.
species.activity: Mostly nocturnal; usually feeds quietly on the forest floor.
species.behaviour: Typically encountered alone while browsing or resting under cover. A published Singapore survey also recorded more than one animal together, so solitary does not mean never seen with another.
species.reproduction: Usually produces one well-developed young. Regional accounts describe a pregnancy of roughly five months; this is not a prediction of Singapore birth dates. Juveniles were documented during the Ubin rediscovery study.
species.singapore: Confirmed on Pulau Ubin in 2008 after a long gap in verified records. NParks still includes the species in its 2025 Ubin conservation work. Its limited Singapore distribution does not mean every suitable mainland forest contains it.
species.ecologicalRole: A forest-floor plant consumer and part of the food web linking vegetation to predators.
species.pressures: Habitat disturbance and fragmentation can affect its restricted local habitat. Hunting is a pressure across its wider range. Protecting forest cover and limiting disturbance support its persistence.
species.watch: Keep to permitted paths, observe quietly and never feed or pursue it. Leave dense undergrowth undisturbed and do not share exact resting locations.

species.name: Horsfield’s flying squirrel
species.fact: Its gliding membrane stretches between all four limbs; the long tail is flattened rather than round and bushy.
species.summary: A nocturnal squirrel that glides between trees on a membrane joining its limbs. Its quiet life above the ground makes it much less conspicuous than the daytime squirrels in parks.
species.identification: Dark brown upperparts, a paler orange-buff or whitish underside and rusty edges to the gliding membrane. A rounded head, large eyes and long, flattened, feather-like tail complete its outline.
species.diet: Mainly fruit, with insects also listed in the NParks species account.
species.activity: Active at night; rests in a tree cavity by day.
species.behaviour: Climbs using sharp claws and spreads its membrane to glide. It depends on trees for feeding, shelter and travel. Detailed social behaviour remains poorly studied.
species.reproduction: Gives birth to live young, but the reviewed species account does not establish its mating system, breeding season or litter size. Values from larger flying squirrels are not substituted.
species.singapore: Recorded in Singapore's central forest reserves and in a wooded nature park outside them. Local records require careful identification; difficulty seeing a nocturnal animal is not a population estimate.
species.ecologicalRole: A canopy fruit consumer that also eats small invertebrates. Its precise contribution to seed dispersal in Singapore has not been quantified in the reviewed sources.

species.name: Malayan porcupine
species.fact: Porcupines cannot shoot their quills. A quill can detach after contact, which helps explain the familiar myth.
species.summary: A large ground-dwelling rodent with striking defensive quills. Camera traps helped establish that this secretive native mammal still survived in Singapore after decades with few reports.
species.identification: A blunt muzzle, stout body, short legs and a short tail. The longest back quills are strongly patterned in black and white. It is a porcupine, not a hedgehog.
species.diet: Fruit, roots and stems, gathered while foraging on the ground.
species.activity: Nocturnal; normally shelters in burrows during daylight.
species.behaviour: Digs burrows and travels on land. A threatened animal can raise its quills, rattle its tail and back towards a threat; leave it room to retreat.
species.reproduction: Gives birth to live young. The Singapore field sources reviewed here do not establish a local breeding season or typical litter size, so no exact reproductive timetable is claimed.
species.singapore: Rediscovered on an offshore island in 2005. Later camera-trap records documented animals in mainland forest reserves and other wooded areas. RDB3 continues to recognise a native, nationally Critically Endangered population.
species.ecologicalRole: Its plant feeding links roots, stems and fallen fruit to the forest food web; burrowing also disturbs small patches of soil.
species.pressures: Forest loss and fragmentation reduce habitat. Hunting for meat and trade in body parts are documented regional pressures; the reviewed sources do not provide a current Singapore hunting rate.
species.watch: Keep a generous distance and never block its path or approach a burrow. Do not attempt to handle an animal or remove its quills.

species.name: Red-cheeked flying squirrel
species.fact: Its broad, flattened tail gives the group its 'arrow-tailed flying squirrel' nickname.
species.summary: A tiny forest squirrel with warm-coloured cheeks and a broad gliding membrane. It is one of Singapore's least conspicuous mammals and needs careful observation to separate it from other gliders.
species.identification: Grey-brown upperparts with rusty colouring, a pale underside, orange-brown cheeks and a flattened tail. NParks describes a narrow white edge along the side of the gliding membrane.
species.diet: Regional observations describe fruit, flowers and leaves, with some insects.
species.activity: Nocturnal and mainly active in trees.
species.behaviour: Glides between trees and shelters in cavities in tall trunks. It appears largely solitary, but detailed social studies are limited.
species.reproduction: Uses sheltered tree holes. Reliable species-specific breeding dates and litter sizes were not established in this review. Frequently repeated numbers in one educational account are actually attributed to a different Hylopetes species.
species.singapore: Recorded from Bukit Timah and Central Catchment forests. The latter records were published in 2013, so the older statement that it occurs only in Bukit Timah is not retained.
species.ecologicalRole: Connects canopy plant resources and small invertebrates with the forest food web. No measured Singapore seed-dispersal rate is claimed.
species.pressures: Loss or degradation of mature forest can remove both food and cavity shelters. Its restricted habitat and small size also make monitoring difficult.
species.watch: Watch quietly from open trails without flash or prolonged direct light. Do not inspect occupied tree cavities or publish exact shelter locations.

species.name: Red-cheeked flying squirrel
species.fact: Its broad, flattened tail gives the group its 'arrow-tailed flying squirrel' nickname.
species.summary: A tiny forest squirrel with warm-coloured cheeks and a broad gliding membrane. It is one of Singapore's least conspicuous mammals and needs careful observation to separate it from other gliders.
species.identification: Grey-brown upperparts with rusty colouring, a pale underside, orange-brown cheeks and a flattened tail. NParks describes a narrow white edge along the side of the gliding membrane.
species.diet: Regional observations describe fruit, flowers and leaves, with some insects.
species.activity: Nocturnal and mainly active in trees.
species.behaviour: Glides between trees and shelters in cavities in tall trunks. It appears largely solitary, but detailed social studies are limited.
species.reproduction: Uses sheltered tree holes. Reliable species-specific breeding dates and litter sizes were not established in this review. Frequently repeated numbers in one educational account are actually attributed to a different Hylopetes species.
species.singapore: Recorded from Bukit Timah and Central Catchment forests. The latter records were published in 2013, so the older statement that it occurs only in Bukit Timah is not retained.
species.ecologicalRole: Connects canopy plant resources and small invertebrates with the forest food web. No measured Singapore seed-dispersal rate is claimed.
species.pressures: Loss or degradation of mature forest can remove both food and cavity shelters. Its restricted habitat and small size also make monitoring difficult.
species.watch: Watch quietly from open trails without flash or prolonged direct light. Do not inspect occupied tree cavities or publish exact shelter locations.

species.name: Small-toothed palm civet
species.fact: A published Singapore record describes two civets resting against each other in the canopy; the observers could not confirm their relationship.
species.summary: A canopy-dwelling civet that is much less often seen than Singapore's familiar Sumatran palm civet. Published observations of adults and apparent young show how much remains to learn about its forest life.
species.identification: Usually brownish-grey with a darker face and tail, pale forehead marking and three dark lines along the back. Markings vary, so a quick glimpse is insufficient to identify an unfamiliar civet confidently.
species.diet: Fruit is important, alongside insects and small vertebrates. It belongs to the carnivore order but has an omnivorous diet.
species.activity: Nocturnal and strongly arboreal; often rests high in vegetation.
species.behaviour: Often described as solitary. Singapore observers have also recorded pairs resting close together, although their ages and relationship could not always be confirmed.
species.reproduction: Females produce and nurse dependent young. Published Singapore sightings include an apparent juvenile, but those observations do not establish a breeding season or confirm that every pair is a mother and offspring.
species.singapore: Associated with the central nature reserves. A 2023 NUS biodiversity record documents observations in secondary forest during 2022–2023. Exact resting trees are omitted from this guide.
species.ecologicalRole: A fruit eater and predator of small animals. Seed transport is a plausible ecological contribution, but the profile does not claim a measured local dispersal rate or a demonstrated keystone role.
species.pressures: Forest loss and degradation affect canopy habitat. The reviewed literature describes hunting and capture elsewhere in its range; it does not quantify current Singapore exploitation.
species.watch: Use binoculars from permitted paths and leave resting animals undisturbed. Never bait, feed, touch or follow a civet into the forest.

before.diet: Searches through leaf litter for worms and other invertebrates.
before.activity: Diurnal: active during daylight, as documented in local forest surveys.
before.behaviour: Forages on the ground and climbs trees. Its ability to use both levels is a useful reminder to look above ground as well as along paths.

before.singapore: NParks describes it as relatively common in suitable habitats, including forest and wooded gardens. This does not mean it is equally frequent in every neighbourhood.
before.ecologicalRole: A predator of small ground-dwelling animals within the leaf-litter food web.
before.pressures: Retaining forest cover, leaf litter and climbing trees helps preserve its habitat. Its local Least Concern label does not remove the need for respectful encounters.
before.watch: Watch from a distance and allow it to pass. Never feed, corner or handle a monitor, and keep pets under control.

before.name: Greater mousedeer
before.fact: The decisive 2008 rediscovery photographs showed the throat and chest markings needed to identify the species.
before.summary: A small hoofed forest browser with a rounded body and very slender legs. Its rediscovery on Pulau Ubin shows why an animal missing from casual sightings is not necessarily gone.
before.identification: Reddish-brown fur, pale underparts and contrasting throat markings. More robust than the lesser mousedeer; useful photographs show the neck and chest, not just apparent size. It has no antlers.
before.diet: Fallen fruit, tender leaves and other low-growing plant material.
before.activity: Mostly nocturnal; usually feeds quietly on the forest floor.
before.behaviour: Typically encountered alone while browsing or resting under cover. A published Singapore survey also recorded more than one animal together, so solitary does not mean never seen with another.
before.reproduction: Usually produces one well-developed young. Regional accounts describe a pregnancy of roughly five months; this is not a prediction of Singapore birth dates. Juveniles were documented during the Ubin rediscovery study.
before.singapore: Confirmed on Pulau Ubin in 2008 after a long gap in verified records. NParks still includes the species in its 2025 Ubin conservation work. Its limited Singapore distribution does not mean every suitable mainland forest contains it.
before.ecologicalRole: A forest-floor plant consumer and part of the food web linking vegetation to predators.
before.pressures: Habitat disturbance and fragmentation can affect its restricted local habitat. Hunting is a pressure across its wider range. Protecting forest cover and limiting disturbance support its persistence.
before.watch: Keep to permitted paths, observe quietly and never feed or pursue it. Leave dense undergrowth undisturbed and do not share exact resting locations.

before.name: Horsfield’s flying squirrel
before.fact: Its gliding membrane stretches between all four limbs; the long tail is flattened rather than round and bushy.
before.summary: A nocturnal squirrel that glides between trees on a membrane joining its limbs. Its quiet life above the ground makes it much less conspicuous than the daytime squirrels in parks.
before.identification: Dark brown upperparts, a paler orange-buff or whitish underside and rusty edges to the gliding membrane. A rounded head, large eyes and long, flattened, feather-like tail complete its outline.
before.diet: Mainly fruit, with insects also listed in the NParks species account.
before.activity: Active at night; rests in a tree cavity by day.
before.behaviour: Climbs using sharp claws and spreads its membrane to glide. It depends on trees for feeding, shelter and travel. Detailed social behaviour remains poorly studied.
before.reproduction: Gives birth to live young, but the reviewed species account does not establish its mating system, breeding season or litter size. Values from larger flying squirrels are not substituted.
before.singapore: Recorded in Singapore's central forest reserves and in a wooded nature park outside them. Local records require careful identification; difficulty seeing a nocturnal animal is not a population estimate.
before.ecologicalRole: A canopy fruit consumer that also eats small invertebrates. Its precise contribution to seed dispersal in Singapore has not been quantified in the reviewed sources.
before.pressures: Loss of forest and suitable cavity-bearing trees removes shelter and foraging areas. Maintaining connected wooded habitat is important for a species that travels between trees.
before.watch: Observe from permitted routes and avoid flash, sustained spotlighting or disturbance of tree holes. Never lure an animal with food or enter closed areas to seek it.

before.name: Malayan porcupine
before.fact: Porcupines cannot shoot their quills. A quill can detach after contact, which helps explain the familiar myth.
before.summary: A large ground-dwelling rodent with striking defensive quills. Camera traps helped establish that this secretive native mammal still survived in Singapore after decades with few reports.
before.identification: A blunt muzzle, stout body, short legs and a short tail. The longest back quills are strongly patterned in black and white. It is a porcupine, not a hedgehog.
before.diet: Fruit, roots and stems, gathered while foraging on the ground.
before.activity: Nocturnal; normally shelters in burrows during daylight.
before.behaviour: Digs burrows and travels on land. A threatened animal can raise its quills, rattle its tail and back towards a threat; leave it room to retreat.
before.reproduction: Gives birth to live young. The Singapore field sources reviewed here do not establish a local breeding season or typical litter size, so no exact reproductive timetable is claimed.
before.singapore: Rediscovered on an offshore island in 2005. Later camera-trap records documented animals in mainland forest reserves and other wooded areas. RDB3 continues to recognise a native, nationally Critically Endangered population.
before.ecologicalRole: Its plant feeding links roots, stems and fallen fruit to the forest food web; burrowing also disturbs small patches of soil.
before.pressures: Forest loss and fragmentation reduce habitat. Hunting for meat and trade in body parts are documented regional pressures; the reviewed sources do not provide a current Singapore hunting rate.
before.watch: Keep a generous distance and never block its path or approach a burrow. Do not attempt to handle an animal or remove its quills.

before.name: Red-cheeked flying squirrel
before.fact: Its broad, flattened tail gives the group its 'arrow-tailed flying squirrel' nickname.
before.summary: A tiny forest squirrel with warm-coloured cheeks and a broad gliding membrane. It is one of Singapore's least conspicuous mammals and needs careful observation to separate it from other gliders.
before.identification: Grey-brown upperparts with rusty colouring, a pale underside, orange-brown cheeks and a flattened tail. NParks describes a narrow white edge along the side of the gliding membrane.
before.diet: Regional observations describe fruit, flowers and leaves, with some insects.
before.activity: Nocturnal and mainly active in trees.
before.behaviour: Glides between trees and shelters in cavities in tall trunks. It appears largely solitary, but detailed social studies are limited.
before.reproduction: Uses sheltered tree holes. Reliable species-specific breeding dates and litter sizes were not established in this review. Frequently repeated numbers in one educational account are actually attributed to a different Hylopetes species.
before.singapore: Recorded from Bukit Timah and Central Catchment forests. The latter records were published in 2013, so the older statement that it occurs only in Bukit Timah is not retained.
before.ecologicalRole: Connects canopy plant resources and small invertebrates with the forest food web. No measured Singapore seed-dispersal rate is claimed.
before.pressures: Loss or degradation of mature forest can remove both food and cavity shelters. Its restricted habitat and small size also make monitoring difficult.
before.watch: Watch quietly from open trails without flash or prolonged direct light. Do not inspect occupied tree cavities or publish exact shelter locations.

before.name: Small-toothed palm civet
before.fact: A published Singapore record describes two civets resting against each other in the canopy; the observers could not confirm their relationship.
before.summary: A canopy-dwelling civet that is much less often seen than Singapore's familiar Sumatran palm civet. Published observations of adults and apparent young show how much remains to learn about its forest life.
before.identification: Usually brownish-grey with a darker face and tail, pale forehead marking and three dark lines along the back. Markings vary, so a quick glimpse is insufficient to identify an unfamiliar civet confidently.
before.diet: Fruit is important, alongside insects and small vertebrates. It belongs to the carnivore order but has an omnivorous diet.
before.activity: Nocturnal and strongly arboreal; often rests high in vegetation.
before.behaviour: Often described as solitary. Singapore observers have also recorded pairs resting close together, although their ages and relationship could not always be confirmed.
before.reproduction: Females produce and nurse dependent young. Published Singapore sightings include an apparent juvenile, but those observations do not establish a breeding season or confirm that every pair is a mother and offspring.
before.singapore: Associated with the central nature reserves. A 2023 NUS biodiversity record documents observations in secondary forest during 2022–2023. Exact resting trees are omitted from this guide.
before.ecologicalRole: A fruit eater and predator of small animals. Seed transport is a plausible ecological contribution, but the profile does not claim a measured local dispersal rate or a demonstrated keystone role.
before.pressures: Forest loss and degradation affect canopy habitat. The reviewed literature describes hunting and capture elsewhere in its range; it does not quantify current Singapore exploitation.
before.watch: Use binoculars from permitted paths and leave resting animals undisturbed. Never bait, feed, touch or follow a civet into the forest.

after.identification: Usually brownish-grey with a darker face and tail, pale forehead marking and three dark lines along the back. Markings vary, so a quick glimpse is insufficient to identify an unfamiliar civet confidently.
after.diet: Fruit is important, alongside insects and small vertebrates. It belongs to the carnivore order but has an omnivorous diet.
after.activity: Nocturnal and strongly arboreal; often rests high in vegetation.
after.behaviour: Often described as solitary. Singapore observers have also recorded pairs resting close together, although their ages and relationship could not always be confirmed.
after.reproduction: Females produce and nurse dependent young. Published Singapore sightings include an apparent juvenile, but those observations do not establish a breeding season or confirm that every pair is a mother and offspring.
after.singapore: Associated with the central nature reserves. A 2023 NUS biodiversity record documents observations in secondary forest during 2022–2023. Exact resting trees are omitted from this guide.
after.ecologicalRole: A fruit eater and predator of small animals. Seed transport is a plausible ecological contribution, but the profile does not claim a measured local dispersal rate or a demonstrated keystone role.
after.pressures: Forest loss and degradation affect canopy habitat. The reviewed literature describes hunting and capture elsewhere in its range; it does not quantify current Singapore exploitation.
after.watch: Use binoculars from permitted paths and leave resting animals undisturbed. Never bait, feed, touch or follow a civet into the forest.
